Exam Essentials.title: The Professional lens: you own it in production
Exam Essentials.desc: Foundations asks whether you can design a working Claude system. Professional asks whether you can own one — ship it, defend the decisions to stakeholders, keep it safe and compliant, and still be responsible for it eighteen months later. Almost every item is written from inside that ownership.
Exam Essentials.note: When two options are both technically sound, pick the one that survives contact with operations: the one that can be audited, monitored, handed over, or rolled back.

Exam Essentials.title: 63 items, 120 minutes, 720 to pass
Exam Essentials.desc: Scored on a 100–1000 scale with a 720 cut, across 7 domains weighted from 7% to 19% — the flattest spread of any Claude certification. Roughly 114 seconds per item, which is generous for recall and tight for a three-way trade-off scenario.
Exam Essentials.note: No domain is skippable. Even Developer Productivity at 7% is ~4 items — more than the margin most people pass by.

Exam Essentials.title: Workflow vs agent is the spine of the exam
Exam Essentials.desc: Workflows run a predefined control flow you wrote. Agents decide their own next step. Agents buy adaptability and pay for it in cost, latency, non-determinism and debugging difficulty. That trade shows up in every domain, not just architecture.
Exam Essentials.note: Default to the most constrained pattern that meets the requirement. Reach for autonomy only when the task genuinely cannot be decomposed in advance — and expect the exam to describe a task that can be.

Exam Essentials.title: Every architecture question is a trade-off question
Exam Essentials.desc: Accuracy, latency, cost and maintainability pull against each other. A CCAR-P stem almost always names which one is binding — a p95 budget, a per-transaction cost ceiling, a regulator's reproducibility requirement, a team of two who must maintain it.
Exam Essentials.note: Find the binding constraint in the stem before reading the options. Options that optimise a dimension the stem never mentioned are distractors.

Exam Essentials.title: "MOST appropriate" means read the constraint, not the concept
Exam Essentials.desc: Several options will describe genuinely good practice. Only one responds to what this scenario actually constrains. The exam tests judgement under specifics, not recall of best-practice lists.
Exam Essentials.note: If you can eliminate an option only by saying "that's less good in general", you probably have the wrong one. The right elimination sounds like "that ignores the 200ms budget".

Exam Essentials.title: Measure before you optimise
Exam Essentials.desc: Evals come before prompt tuning, model downgrades, caching, or any other optimisation. Without a measurement you cannot tell an improvement from a regression, and every subsequent change is guesswork.
Exam Essentials.note: When a stem describes a team about to change something with no eval in place, the answer is usually to build the measurement first — even when a more exciting option is on the list.

Exam Essentials.title: Guardrails are placement decisions
Exam Essentials.desc: The question is rarely whether to validate, but where in the request path — before the model, after it, around tool execution, or at the downstream consumer. Placement determines what class of failure you actually catch.
Exam Essentials.note: Anything that executes, sends, pays, or writes needs a deterministic check outside the model. A model instructed not to do something is a preference; code that refuses is a control.

Exam Essentials.title: Non-determinism changes how you write an SLA
Exam Essentials.desc: You cannot promise a fixed output for a fixed input. You commit to measured accuracy on a defined eval set, latency percentiles, availability, and an escalation path for the cases the system gets wrong — not to correctness per request.
Exam Essentials.note: Any option that promises deterministic per-request correctness from an LLM is wrong, regardless of how well it is hedged.

Exam Essentials.title: Cost means total cost of ownership
Exam Essentials.desc: Token spend is often the smaller number. Human review, retrieval infrastructure, eval maintenance, monitoring, incident response, and the engineering time to keep prompts current usually dominate — and they scale differently from API calls.
Exam Essentials.note: When a stem gives you a cost problem, check whether the expensive thing is actually the model. Frequently the answer is to remove a human review step by raising confidence, not to switch tiers.

Exam Essentials.title: The simplest thing that meets the requirement wins
Exam Essentials.desc: Retrieval before fine-tuning. A prompt before a pipeline. One agent with good tools before a multi-agent system. Added machinery must earn its place against a stated requirement in the stem.
Exam Essentials.note: The most sophisticated option is a distractor more often than it is the key. Ask what requirement the extra complexity satisfies — if you cannot point at one in the stem, it is not the answer.

Integration.title: Retrieval quality gates everything downstream
Integration.desc: In a RAG system, no amount of prompt engineering repairs bad retrieval. If the right passage never enters the context, the model's only options are to hedge or to invent. Diagnose retrieval before you touch the generation prompt.
Integration.note: Split the metrics: retrieval (did the right chunk come back?) and generation (given the right chunk, was the answer faithful?). A stem that reports high retrieval precision is pointing you at the generation half, and vice versa.

Integration.title: Chunking is a recall/precision trade-off
Integration.desc: Small chunks retrieve precisely but arrive without the surrounding context needed to interpret them. Large chunks carry context but dilute the embedding and burn context window on irrelevant text. Overlap mitigates boundary loss at the cost of index size and duplicate hits.
Integration.note: Structure-aware splitting — on sections, clauses, or function boundaries — usually beats a fixed token count. Attaching the parent-section heading as metadata is the cheap fix for lost context.

Integration.title: Hybrid search plus reranking
Integration.desc: Dense vector search captures meaning but misses exact tokens — part numbers, error codes, surnames, statute references. Sparse/BM25 keyword search catches those and misses paraphrase. Hybrid runs both and fuses; a reranker then re-scores the fused shortlist with a model that actually reads query and passage together.
Integration.note: The classic exam scenario: semantic search fails on identifiers. The answer is hybrid retrieval, not a better embedding model.

Integration.title: Tool descriptions are prompt engineering
Integration.desc: A tool's name, description and parameter schema are the entire interface the model reasons over. Ambiguous descriptions, overlapping tools, and untyped free-text parameters cause wrong-tool selection and malformed arguments far more often than model capability does.
Integration.note: When the model picks the wrong tool, the first fix is disambiguating the descriptions and narrowing the schemas — not a bigger model or a longer system prompt.

Integration.title: MCP: tools, resources and prompts are different things
Integration.desc: Model Context Protocol standardises how a client connects to servers that expose capabilities. Tools are model-invoked actions. Resources are application-controlled context the client can attach. Prompts are user-invoked templates. Conflating them produces servers that expose everything as a tool and blow the context budget.
Integration.note: Read-only reference data that the app knows it needs is a resource. Something the model should decide to call is a tool. Transport choice — local stdio vs remote HTTP — is a deployment and trust-boundary decision.

Integration.title: Prompt caching economics
Integration.desc: Caching a stable prefix — system prompt, tool definitions, a large fixed document — lets repeated calls reuse it instead of reprocessing. It pays off when the prefix is large, stable, and reused frequently within the cache lifetime. It does nothing for a prompt whose beginning changes every call.
Integration.note: Cacheable content must sit at the front and be byte-identical. Putting a timestamp or a user ID at the top of an otherwise stable prompt destroys the whole cache.

Integration.title: Batch vs realtime routing
Integration.desc: Asynchronous batch processing trades latency for throughput and cost on workloads where nobody is waiting — overnight enrichment, backfills, bulk classification, periodic re-scoring. Interactive paths cannot use it.
Integration.note: A stem that says "results are reviewed the next morning" is telling you the workload is batch-eligible. Look for the absence of a waiting human.

Integration.title: Streaming changes your error model
Integration.desc: Server-sent events give the user first tokens quickly, which improves perceived latency enormously. But you have committed to output before you have seen all of it — post-hoc validation, guardrail filtering and schema checking all get harder once bytes are on the wire.
Integration.note: Streaming and output guardrails are in tension. If a stem requires content to be screened before the user sees it, streaming the raw output to the client is wrong.

Integration.title: Retries need idempotency
Integration.desc: Rate limits, timeouts and transient errors demand retry with exponential backoff and jitter. But a retried request that already had a side effect — a payment, an email, a ticket — duplicates it. Idempotency keys and a deduplication store make retries safe.
Integration.note: Retry logic in front of tool calls that mutate state is a trap unless the tool is idempotent. Jitter matters: synchronised retries from many clients rebuild the spike that caused the failure.

Integration.title: First-party API vs Bedrock vs Vertex
Integration.desc: Claude is available through Anthropic's own API and through cloud marketplaces. The choice is usually driven by non-technical factors: existing cloud commitments and billing, data residency, network isolation, procurement, and which compliance evidence the organisation already holds for that platform.
Integration.note: When a stem emphasises an existing enterprise agreement, VPC-only networking, or a regional data requirement, it is steering you to the cloud-hosted route — not because the model differs.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: The augmented LLM is the baseline unit
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: A model with retrieval, tools and memory attached is the building block every larger pattern composes. Before designing anything multi-step, establish whether one well-equipped call already meets the requirement.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: A surprising number of scenarios are solved by giving one call better context and better tools. Complexity should be forced by a requirement, not assumed.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Workflow vs agent
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: Workflows follow a control flow you defined; agents choose their own path. Agents handle open-ended tasks whose steps cannot be enumerated in advance, and pay in cost, latency, variance, and difficulty of testing and audit.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: Regulated, high-volume, latency-sensitive or auditable work pushes toward workflows. Genuinely unpredictable, low-volume, exploratory work justifies agents.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: The workflow patterns worth knowing cold
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: Prompt chaining decomposes a task into ordered steps with checks between them. Routing classifies input and dispatches to a specialised handler. Parallelisation splits work into independent sections, or runs the same task several times and votes. Each has a distinct signature in a scenario.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: Sectioning parallelises different subtasks; voting runs the same subtask repeatedly for confidence. A stem worried about false negatives on a safety check is describing voting.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Orchestrator–workers
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: A central model decomposes a task at runtime, dispatches subtasks to workers, and synthesises the results. Unlike static parallelisation, the number and nature of subtasks is not known until the input is seen.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: The distinguishing question is whether the decomposition is fixed at design time (parallelisation) or decided per input (orchestrator–workers).

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Evaluator–optimiser loops
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: One call generates, a second critiques against explicit criteria, the first revises. It works when there are articulable quality criteria and iteration measurably helps — translation nuance, code that must pass tests, writing against a rubric.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: It requires a bounded loop count and a stopping condition. An unbounded critique loop is a cost incident waiting to happen.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Multi-agent costs coordination, not just tokens
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: Multiple agents multiply token consumption, add handoff latency, and create failure modes that do not exist in a single agent: lost context at boundaries, conflicting conclusions, and errors that propagate silently downstream.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: Multi-agent earns its place when subtasks are genuinely parallel, need isolated context, or need different tools and permissions — not merely because a task has several steps.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Context isolation is the real argument for subagents
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: The strongest reason to split work across agents is often not parallelism but context hygiene: each agent sees only what its subtask requires, so a long exploratory search does not pollute the context of the agent doing the final synthesis.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: Frame subagents as a context-engineering tool. The parent gets a clean summary instead of the full transcript of how it was produced.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Decompose the latency budget
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: End-to-end latency is retrieval plus model time plus tool calls plus network plus any serial dependency between them. Model time is driven far more by output tokens than input tokens. You cannot optimise what you have not attributed.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: When a stem gives a p95 budget, mentally allocate it across stages. The fix is usually removing a serial hop or shortening the output, not switching model tier.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Mix model tiers within one system
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: Tier selection is a per-subtask decision, not a per-system one. Cheap fast models handle classification, routing, extraction and filtering; the expensive tier is reserved for the step where reasoning quality actually determines the outcome.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: A routing layer on a small model in front of a capable model is one of the highest-leverage cost patterns, and a very common correct answer.

Solution Design & Architecture.title: Human-in-the-loop is a placement decision
Solution Design & Architecture.desc: Review can sit before an action executes, after output is generated but before release, on a sample for quality assurance, or only on low-confidence cases. Each placement catches different failures and costs different amounts of human time.
Solution Design & Architecture.note: Confidence-triggered review — humans see only the uncertain cases — is how you keep a review budget finite as volume grows. Reviewing everything does not scale and usually is not the intended answer.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: Eval-driven development
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Write the evaluation before the optimisation. A representative eval set with a defined metric converts subjective argument about whether the system got better into a number, and makes regressions visible before users find them.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: The order is: define success, build the eval set, measure the baseline, then change one thing. A scenario where a team is tuning prompts with no eval has an obvious first move.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: Golden datasets must mirror production
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: An eval set assembled from easy or convenient cases produces a number that does not predict production behaviour. It needs the real distribution — including the messy inputs, the edge cases, the ambiguous ones, and the cases the system currently fails.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: Mine production traffic and escalations for eval cases. An eval set that only contains cases you already pass measures nothing.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: LLM-as-judge and its biases
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Using a model to grade outputs scales evaluation far beyond human throughput, but judges carry known biases: they favour longer answers, they are sensitive to the order options are presented in, and they tend to prefer text from the same model family.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: Mitigate with an explicit rubric, position randomisation or swapping, and calibration against human labels. A judge with no rubric is a vibe check with extra steps.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: Validate the grader itself
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Before trusting an automated grader, measure its agreement with human judgement on a labelled subset. An unvalidated judge can be confidently wrong in a consistent direction, which is worse than no measurement because it manufactures false confidence.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: If a scenario reports that eval scores improved but users complain more, suspect the grader before the system.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: RAG needs its own metrics
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Retrieval and generation fail differently and must be measured separately. Context precision and recall assess whether retrieval found the right material; faithfulness assesses whether the answer is actually grounded in what was retrieved; answer relevance assesses whether it addressed the question.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: High faithfulness with low answer relevance means the model is faithfully summarising the wrong passages — a retrieval problem wearing a generation costume.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: Trajectory vs outcome evaluation
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: For agents, the final answer is not the whole story. An agent can reach a correct result through an unsafe, expensive or lucky path. Trajectory evaluation inspects the sequence of tool calls and intermediate decisions.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: When a stem mentions unpredictable cost, wasted tool calls, or an agent that sometimes gets there the wrong way, outcome-only evaluation is the gap.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: Regression gates in CI
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Prompts, tool schemas, retrieval configuration and model versions are all deployable artefacts and all can regress. Running the eval suite in continuous integration and blocking merges that drop below a threshold is how you stop silent quality decay.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: Pin model versions in production. An unpinned model that updates underneath you changes behaviour without a deploy, and nothing in your change log explains it.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: A/B testing and significance
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Comparing two prompts or two models on a handful of examples produces noise, not evidence. You need enough samples for the difference you care about, held-out data, and awareness that variance in a stochastic system is real.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: Beware of tuning against the eval set until it is memorised. Keep a held-out set the optimisation loop never sees.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: What to monitor in production
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Latency percentiles rather than averages, error and refusal rates, cost per completed task rather than per call, tool-call failure rates, retrieval hit rates, and a quality proxy such as user correction, escalation, or thumbs-down rate.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: Cost per successful task is the honest metric. Cost per API call hides a system that is cheap per call and retries four times.

Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.title: The optimisation order
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.desc: Establish the measurement, then find where the time and money actually go, then fix the dominant term. Common levers in rough order of yield: shorten outputs, cache stable prefixes, move eligible work to batch, route easy cases to a cheaper tier, and only then re-engineer the architecture.
Evaluation, Testing & Optimisation.note: Downgrading the model tier without an eval gate is the classic wrong answer — it saves money and quietly loses accuracy nobody is measuring.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Indirect prompt injection is the architectural one
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: Direct injection is a user typing an attack. Indirect injection hides instructions in content the system retrieves and trusts — a document, a web page, a ticket comment, a tool result. The model cannot reliably distinguish retrieved data from instructions, so the architecture must.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: The moment a system both reads untrusted content and holds a tool that can act, injection becomes a live risk. Untrusted content should be delimited, and consequential actions should require confirmation outside the model.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Guardrails on both sides
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: Input guardrails screen for injection, prohibited requests and PII before the call. Output guardrails check for policy violations, leaked sensitive data, unsupported claims and malformed structure before the response reaches a user or a downstream system.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: Deterministic checks outside the model are controls; instructions inside the prompt are preferences. Regulators and incident reviews care about the difference.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Least privilege for tools and data
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: A tool the model can call runs with whatever permissions you gave it. Scope credentials to the minimum, prefer read-only where possible, separate the tools that read from the tools that write, and never hand an agent broad standing access because it is convenient.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: Tool permissions should reflect the *user's* entitlement, not the service account's. Otherwise the model becomes a route to data the user could never reach directly.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: The confused deputy
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: The system acts with its own elevated authority on behalf of a user who lacks it. An assistant with database access answering "show me all salaries" is the canonical case: the model is not malicious, it is being used as a deputy with more privilege than the requester.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: Authorise at the data layer against the end user's identity. Filtering in the prompt is not access control.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Data minimisation beats data protection
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: The strongest privacy control is not sending the data at all. Redact or tokenise identifiers before the call, send only the fields the task needs, and re-attach identifiers afterwards if the output requires them.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: Where a stem raises PII, look for the option that reduces what leaves the boundary rather than the one that adds a control around sending everything.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: EU AI Act risk tiers
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: Obligations scale with a system's risk classification — from prohibited practices, through high-risk uses that carry conformity, documentation, human-oversight and logging duties, down to limited-risk transparency obligations and minimal-risk uses.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: Employment, credit, education, essential services and law enforcement uses tend to land in the high-risk tier. Classification drives the controls, so establish it during discovery, not after launch.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Model risk management in regulated sectors
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: Financial services and healthcare apply existing model-governance regimes to AI systems: documented purpose and limitations, independent validation, ongoing performance monitoring, defined human accountability, and a change-control process.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: "Who is accountable for a wrong decision, and can they explain it?" is a governance question the exam asks in architectural clothing. The answer is never "the model".

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Log for reproducibility, not just debugging
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: When a decision must be defensible years later, you need the inputs, retrieved context, prompt version, model version, parameters and output — not merely the final answer. Reconstructing why a system said something is impossible from the output alone.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: A stem that mentions a multi-year audit or reproducibility requirement is asking about capturing the full decision record, including which prompt and model version ran.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: Retention and training-data commitments
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: Enterprise deployments care intensely about whether inputs are retained and whether they are used for training. Zero-retention arrangements and contractual training exclusions are frequently the blocking issue in a regulated procurement.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: Know that these are contractual and configuration matters to be established during discovery. Do not guess at specific default retention periods.

Governance, Safety & Risk Management.title: AI incidents need their own runbook
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.desc: An AI failure often is not an outage — the system is up and confidently wrong. Detection depends on quality signals rather than error rates, and containment options include reverting a prompt, pinning back a model version, tightening a guardrail, or routing to human review.
Governance, Safety & Risk Management.note: The ability to roll back a prompt independently of a code deploy is a real architectural requirement, and a common correct answer.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Discovery before design
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: Structured discovery establishes the actual business outcome, who is affected, what the current process costs, what accuracy is genuinely required, and what constraints are non-negotiable. Skipping it produces technically elegant systems that solve the wrong problem.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: When a stakeholder arrives asking for a specific solution, the professional move is to establish the underlying outcome first — without being obstructive about it.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Baseline before build
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: If you do not know how accurate, fast or expensive the current process is, you cannot demonstrate improvement, set a meaningful target, or justify the spend. The baseline is also usually worse than stakeholders believe, which helps.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: "Improve accuracy" is not a requirement. "Raise first-pass accuracy from the measured 71% to 90% at no more than current cost per case" is.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Is this even an LLM problem?
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: Deterministic rules, existing search, classical ML, or fixing the upstream data are frequently better answers. An LLM is the right tool for unstructured language, ambiguity and generation — not for arithmetic, exact lookup, or anything requiring guaranteed consistency.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: A genuinely senior answer sometimes recommends not using Claude for a component. The exam does reward this.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Architecture decision records
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: An ADR captures the decision, the context that forced it, the options considered, and the consequences accepted. Its value arrives eighteen months later, when someone asks why the system works this way and everyone involved has moved on.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: Record the rejected options and why. An ADR without the alternatives is a description, not a decision record.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Executive versus technical framing
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: Executives need the decision, the business consequence, the cost, the risk and what you need from them. Engineers need the mechanism and the trade-off. The same architecture requires two genuinely different narratives — not the same deck read slower.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: Lead with the recommendation and its consequence for a leadership audience. Options that involve walking executives through implementation detail are usually distractors.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: SLAs for probabilistic systems
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: Commit to availability, latency percentiles, and measured accuracy against a defined eval set with a defined refresh cadence — plus what happens when the system is wrong. Never commit to per-request correctness.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: Always negotiate the escalation and remediation path alongside the number. The handling of the failure cases is the part stakeholders actually experience.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: TCO beyond token spend
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: A credible cost case includes inference, retrieval infrastructure, human review, eval maintenance, monitoring, incident response, and the engineering time to keep prompts and evals current as the world changes. Ongoing maintenance is the line most often omitted.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: When a business case looks too good, the missing line is almost always human review or maintenance. Both scale with volume and with change.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Pilot-to-production criteria, agreed in advance
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: Define before the pilot starts what result justifies proceeding: accuracy threshold on a held-out set, cost per case, latency, user acceptance, and the controls that must be in place. Otherwise the decision becomes a matter of enthusiasm.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: A pilot without pre-agreed success criteria always succeeds, which is exactly why it is worthless as evidence.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Handoff and runbooks
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: A system handed to a run team needs documented architecture, known failure modes and their symptoms, escalation paths, the monitoring dashboard and what normal looks like on it, and instructions for changing prompts safely.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: "How does the on-call engineer who has never seen this system diagnose it at 3am?" is the test of whether handoff documentation is real.

Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.title: Versioning, deprecation and migration
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.desc: Prompts and model versions change, requirements drift, and eventually the system is replaced. Plan version pinning, a migration path, a parallel-run period, and a communicated deprecation timeline as part of the original design.
Stakeholder Communication & Lifecycle Ma.note: Parallel-running old and new on live traffic — comparing outputs before switching — is the standard low-risk migration for a system whose failures are expensive.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Choose a tier per subtask
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Haiku, Sonnet and Opus trade cost and latency against reasoning capability. The architectural move is to assign a tier to each step rather than to the whole system: cheap models for classification, extraction, routing and filtering; the capable tier where reasoning determines the outcome.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Prototype on the capable tier to establish what good looks like, then downgrade individual steps behind an eval gate that proves quality held.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Extended thinking, and when it pays
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Allocating a reasoning budget before the answer helps on genuinely hard multi-step problems — complex analysis, difficult debugging, layered constraints. It costs tokens and latency, and it does not improve simple extraction or formatting.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Spending a reasoning budget on a task the model already does reliably is pure cost. Match the budget to problem difficulty, not to importance.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Structure the prompt so the model can parse it
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Long prompts mixing instructions, examples, retrieved documents and user input need explicit boundaries. XML-style tags or clear delimiters let the model tell the parts apart, and let you reference them precisely in your instructions.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Delimiting retrieved and user-supplied content is also a safety measure — it is the foundation for telling the model which regions are data rather than instructions.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Few-shot examples: selection over quantity
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: A handful of well-chosen examples covering the real variety — including edge cases and the format you want — outperforms a long list of near-identical easy ones. Examples teach format and boundary behaviour better than prose describing them.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: If outputs drift in format, add an example of the format rather than another sentence insisting on it. Examples also consume context, so they are a budget item.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Prefill to constrain the opening
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Seeding the start of the assistant's response steers format and skips preamble. It is a cheap, reliable lever for eliminating conversational throat-clearing and forcing the response to begin in a specific shape.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Useful when downstream code parses the output and a friendly introductory sentence breaks the parser.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Structured output via tool schemas
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: When output must be machine-readable, defining a schema the model fills is far more reliable than asking for JSON in prose. You still validate on receipt — schema conformance is not semantic correctness.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Asking politely for valid JSON is the weakest option available. Any stem where downstream parsing is failing is pointing at schema enforcement plus validation.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Context rot
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: A large context window is a budget, not a target. As context grows, attention spreads and relevant material competes with irrelevant material; performance on the actual task degrades even though nothing exceeded a limit.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: "It fits" is not a reason to include something. Curating a smaller, highly relevant context routinely beats stuffing the window.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Compaction and summarisation
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Long-running conversations and agent loops eventually outgrow the window. Compaction summarises earlier turns into a compressed state that preserves decisions, constraints and open threads while discarding transcript detail.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: What you choose to preserve is the design decision. Losing a constraint agreed twenty turns ago is the failure mode this creates.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Just-in-time context
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Rather than front-loading everything the task might need, give the model the means to fetch what it turns out to need — retrieval, a lookup tool, a file reader. Context is assembled on demand instead of pre-loaded on speculation.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Trades a little latency per fetch for a much cleaner context. It is also how you handle corpora that could never fit in the window regardless of size.

Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.title: Prompts are versioned artefacts
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.desc: Production prompts belong in version control, with a change history, an eval run behind each change, and the ability to roll back independently of application code. Prompts edited live in a console are an unauditable production dependency.
Claude Models, Prompting & Context Engin.note: Log which prompt version produced which output. Without it, you cannot investigate a quality regression or reproduce a past decision.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: CLAUDE.md and the memory hierarchy
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Project-level instruction files give Claude Code durable context about a codebase — conventions, architecture, commands, constraints — so it does not have to be re-explained every session. Enterprise, project and personal scopes layer together.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: Anything that must hold across sessions belongs in a file, not in a chat message. Team-wide standards go in the shared project file; personal preferences stay in the user scope.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Settings precedence
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Configuration resolves through a defined hierarchy, with organisation-managed policy at the top, then project settings shared with the team, then personal settings. This is what lets a security team set a floor that individuals cannot lower.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: When a scenario asks how to enforce something across every developer regardless of local configuration, the answer is the managed enterprise layer.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Permissions and safe autonomy
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Allow and deny rules govern which tools and commands run without asking. Well-chosen rules remove friction on safe, frequent operations while keeping a human gate on anything destructive or outbound.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: The goal is not maximum autonomy. It is autonomy on the reversible operations and confirmation on the irreversible ones.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Hooks
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Shell commands bound to lifecycle events turn a convention into a guarantee — formatting, linting, secret scanning, or blocking an edit to a protected path. Unlike an instruction in a prompt, a hook runs deterministically.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: When a stem says a rule is "usually followed but sometimes missed", it is asking for deterministic enforcement rather than a better instruction.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Subagents for context isolation
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Delegating a bounded task to a subagent keeps its exploration out of the main context. The parent receives a result rather than the full transcript of how it was reached, which preserves the main thread for the actual work.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: Best for wide searches, audits and independent investigations whose intermediate output is large and whose conclusion is small.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Skills and slash commands
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Packaged, reusable instruction sets encode a team's repeated workflows — a deployment procedure, a review checklist, a repo-specific process — so the same sequence runs the same way regardless of who invokes it.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: The productivity argument is consistency, not speed. It removes the variance between the engineer who knows the procedure and the one who does not.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Headless mode and CI
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Non-interactive invocation lets the same tooling run inside pipelines — triage, automated review, migration passes, documentation generation — with output consumed programmatically rather than read by a person.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: Automation needs tighter permissions than interactive use, not looser, because there is no human watching to catch a bad step.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: MCP server scope
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Servers can be configured for a single user, shared with a project, or managed centrally. Scope determines who gets the capability, who can change it, and how credentials are supplied — which makes it a security decision as much as a convenience one.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: A team-shared server configuration that requires each developer to supply their own credentials is the usual pattern for tools touching production systems.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Tracing a multi-step chain
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Debugging an AI feature requires seeing the whole chain: the input, retrieved context, each prompt and its version, tool calls with arguments and results, and the final output — correlated by a single request identifier.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: Logging only the final response makes non-deterministic failures effectively undiagnosable. Capture enough to replay the request.

Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.title: Cost visibility per team
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.desc: Without attribution, AI spend is a single unexplainable line item. Tagging usage by team, feature and environment turns it into something owners can act on, and makes runaway loops visible before the invoice does.
Developer Productivity & Operational Ena.note: Alert on unusual patterns, not just totals — a retry storm or an unbounded agent loop shows up as anomalous call volume long before month-end.
